items.title: Sailing along a constant compass bearing draws a spiral around the pole
items.claim: A 'rhumb line' (loxodrome) is a path that crosses every meridian at the same angle — what you sail if you hold a constant compass course. Except for due east/west (the equator) or due north/south, a rhumb line spirals around the pole, eventually reaching it after infinite winding.
items.prompt: Why doesn't a constant bearing give a great circle?

options.text: Great circles change bearing as you traverse them (except along the equator or meridians); to maintain a constant compass bearing, you must follow a different curve that spirals — the loxodrome
It only happens near the pole

items.reveal:
A loxodrome (rhumb line) is the curve that intersects all meridians at the same angle. On a sphere, this is an equiangular spiral.

For any constant bearing not aligned with the equator or a meridian, the path spirals around the pole. The length to reach the pole is finite (the spiral converges) but the number of windings is infinite.

On a Mercator projection, rhumb lines appear as straight lines — this is the property Mercator designed his projection for in 1569. Hold a ruler against a Mercator chart and you have a constant compass bearing course.

Great circles, by contrast, appear as curves on Mercator maps, generally bowed toward the nearer pole. Modern aviation uses great-circle routes; old-school open-ocean sailing used rhumb lines (easier to navigate without constant heading recalculation).

In practice: long-distance navigation often combines them — fly an approximate great circle, but compute waypoints at intervals (e.g., every 5 degrees of longitude) and sail rhumb lines between waypoints. This is 'composite sailing'.

The loxodrome was first studied by the Portuguese navigator Pedro Nunes (1537). It contributed to the systematic mathematisation of navigation in the Age of Discovery.
items.why: Compasses point to magnetic north. Holding a constant bearing draws a curve that no Euclidean intuition prepares you for — and the difference between loxodrome and great circle has shaped maps, navigation, and naval strategy for centuries.

items.title: 0.9999... equals 1, exactly
items.claim: The decimal expansion 0.999... (infinitely many 9s) does not approach 1 — it IS 1. Two different decimal expansions can represent the same real number.

options.text: They're approximately equal but slightly different
They have zero difference (1 - 0.999... = 0); 0.999... = sum of 9/10 to the n for n from 1 to infinity = 9/10 / (1 - 1/10) = 1 exactly

items.reveal:
Every infinite decimal expansion is, by definition, a convergent series.
0.999... = 9/10 + 9/100 + 9/1000 + ...
     = 9/10 * (1 + 1/10 + 1/100 + ...)
     = 9/10 * 1/(1 - 1/10)
     = 9/10 * 10/9
     = 1

Another argument: let x = 0.999... Then 10x = 9.999... Subtract: 10x - x = 9.999... - 0.999... so 9x = 9 and x = 1.

Third argument: the difference 1 - 0.999... is less than 10 to the minus n for every n. The only non-negative real with this property is 0. So 1 - 0.999... = 0 and 0.999... = 1.

Decimals are a representation, not an identity. Any real with a terminating decimal also has a 999...-style alternative: 0.5 = 0.4999..., 1 = 0.999..., 0.123 = 0.122999... The two representations are equal.

In educational settings this is one of the most strongly contested results — students often refuse to accept it. The objection is usually based on confusing representations with the numbers themselves.
items.why: Decimals feel like unique addresses for numbers. They are not — every terminating decimal has a recurring-9 twin, and equality of the two is logically forced.

items.title: Integration by parts is the product rule played backwards
items.claim: The product rule: d(uv)/dx = u'v + uv'. Rearrange: uv' = d(uv)/dx - u'v. Integrate: integral of uv' dx = uv - integral of u'v dx. The formula isn't a separate tool — it's the product rule, integrated.

options.text: Choose u as the type higher in 'ILATE' priority: Inverse trig, Logarithmic, Algebraic, Trigonometric, Exponential. These tend to become simpler when differentiated; choosing them as u makes u'v easier to integrate than the original

items.reveal_title: Integration by parts and clever choices
items.reveal:
Integration by parts: integral of u dv = uv - integral of v du.

The formula always works mathematically, but the resulting integral can be HARDER than the original if you choose u and dv poorly. The ILATE heuristic helps:
- I: Inverse trig (arctan, arcsin)
- L: Logarithmic (ln x)
- A: Algebraic (polynomials)
- T: Trigonometric (sin, cos)
- E: Exponential (e^x)

Choose u as the FIRST function appearing in this list. Choose dv as the LAST.

Why: logarithmic and inverse trig functions become algebraic when differentiated; polynomials become lower-degree polynomials. Exponentials and most trig functions stay similar under differentiation, so we'd rather integrate them.

Classical applications:
- integral of x e^x dx: u = x, dv = e^x dx. Result: x e^x - e^x + C.
- integral of x sin x dx: u = x, dv = sin x dx. Result: -x cos x + sin x + C.
- integral of ln x dx: u = ln x, dv = dx. Result: x ln x - x + C.
- integral of x^2 e^x dx: apply twice.

Tabular integration (D-I tabular method) systematises repeated applications.

The Frullani integral, Bessel functions, and many special-function identities come from clever integration by parts. It's not just a textbook drill; it's the algebraic shadow of one of the deepest theorems in calculus (the fundamental theorem applied to product structures).
items.why: Integration by parts is taught as a mechanical technique. It's the product rule running backwards — and the ILATE heuristic is empirical wisdom about which functions are easier to differentiate than integrate.
